Data center fee: household dividend and a public fund

A per-kilowatt-hour fee on electricity used by data centers, split two ways. Part is paid to households as a dividend. The rest goes to a national public fund, using the same national carve-out the expert tool already offers, and the fund is divided among priorities. Move the dials to see the trade-offs. Revenue comes from the data center fee tool's own calculation, unchanged.

Where the numbers come from

This page stacks three layers of data. Each section below is tagged with the layer it uses.

Layer 1 The fee and the dividend Taken unchanged from the data center fee tool (open it), which has its own sources page.
  • Data centers under construction: dcmap.us
  • Fossil and clean share of each state's grid: EPA eGRID 2023
  • On-site gas generation: Global Energy Monitor
  • Households and energy burden by state: DOE LEAD 2022, EIA Form 861
  • Fee rates and load factor: dials you set
Layer 2 What the fund could pay for Added on this page, for comparison only.
  • What programs get today: USAspending.gov, FY2025
  • ACA premium credits: CBO, Sept. 2025
  • Community Health Center Fund: HHS FY2027 budget justification
  • LIHEAP gap: HHS, via the fee tool
  • How the fund is split, return and payout: dials you set
Layer 3 States and districts Added on this page. Breaks layers 1 and 2 down by place.
  • Households and energy burden by census tract: DOE LEAD 2022
  • Tracts to 119th Congress districts: U.S. Census Bureau
  • Program spending by district: USAspending.gov, FY2025

Layer 1 and layer 3 both use DOE LEAD 2022, at different levels (state and census tract), and they agree: the 436 districts add up to the fee tool's national household and burden counts within 0.01%.

How this page is built

Generated by build-fund.py from fund-shell.html plus the calculation core of data-center-tax-tool-by-state.html, copied verbatim. National revenue and the household dividend come from that core's own national aggregate, with its national carve-out set to the fund share. Program benchmarks come from sources/19-priority-benchmarks/benchmarks.csv; a benchmark is shown only if it checks against a saved file: a quoted passage found in a saved document, or an amount matching a saved USAspending.gov response. Otherwise it reads NEEDS SOURCE.

Questions and answers

Where does the money come from?

A fee on every kilowatt-hour of electricity data centers use. Fossil electricity pays the full rate; clean electricity, verified hour by hour, pays a lower one (set by the fossil-to-clean ratio dial). The revenue figure at the top comes from the data center fee tool's own calculation, summed across all 50 states and DC.

Isn't this just a tax?

In law it is an excise. On this page it is called a fee, and the payment to households a dividend, because the money is paid back out rather than kept by the government.

Who gets the dividend, and how much?

It depends on the "Who receives the dividend" setting. By default every household receives something, and households that spend the most of their income on energy receive more: severely burdened households (over 10% of income) get twice a standard share, moderately burdened households (6 to 10%) one share, and everyone else half a share. The table under "The household dividend" shows the amounts at your current settings.

What does the household dividend floor do?

It sets the minimum share of revenue that goes straight to households. Whatever is left goes to the public fund. At 100%, there is no fund and the page matches the data center fee tool exactly. Lower it and the dividend shrinks while the fund grows; the "With no fund" column shows what households give up.

What is the difference between "Spend each year" and "Endowment"?

Spend each year sends the fund's money to the priorities as it comes in. Endowment saves it in a permanent fund and spends only the fund's yearly payout, so priorities get less at first and more later, and the savings are kept. The chart shows when the endowment's payout passes the spend-each-year amount.

Are the return and payout rates realistic?

They are dials for you to set, not sourced figures, and the page marks them NEEDS SOURCE. The defaults (a 5% return after inflation and a 5% payout) mean the fund spends what it earns, so its balance grows only from new fee money. Try a lower return to see the endowment pay less than spending each year would.

How do I read the program rows under "What the fund pays for"?

Each row asks one question: if all of this priority's money went to that single program, how big would it be next to what the program gets today? The rows are alternatives, not a split, so they do not add up. A figure like 17.1× means the money is 17 times the program's current size.

How does new fund money reach my district?

In three steps. First, the fund is split among priorities by the priority dials. Second, each priority's money is divided among states in proportion to what each state receives from that program today. Third, each state's share is divided among its districts by their number of energy-burdened households. Energy assistance skips the second step and is divided nationally by burdened households. This is an illustration of new money following today's funding patterns, not a formula in law; Congress would decide the real one.

Why does my district show $0 for a program its state clearly receives?

Federal spending records place a grant where the grantee is located. Statewide grants, such as child care block grants, go to a state agency, so they show up in the district where that agency sits. That is why each program row also shows the whole state, and why the district estimate uses burdened households rather than the grantee's address.

What about census tracts that cross a district line?

About 5% of tracts do. Their households are divided between districts by land area, the only measure the Census relationship file provides. The district note says how many split tracts your district has.

Why do district totals differ slightly from the data center fee tool?

The data center fee tool stores each state's burdened share rounded to four decimals; the district figures use the unrounded counts. Across the country the difference is under 0.01%, and the page's checks confirm it stays that small.

What happens to the health center fund?

According to HHS's FY2027 budget justification, the mandatory Community Health Center Fund is funded only through December 31, 2026. A permanent revenue source is one way to replace a stream that otherwise needs renewing.

Does this assume data centers keep building at the same pace?

Yes. No behavioral response is assumed: data centers build the same amount with or without the fee, and the endowment holds revenue at today's buildout every year. The data center fee tool has an elasticity dial for testing a price response.

Where do the numbers come from, and how are they checked?

Every figure traces to a file saved in the project's sources folder: DOE LEAD energy burden data, Census district files, USAspending.gov program spending, CBO and HHS documents, and the data center fee tool's own data. Each program figure is checked against its saved file whenever the page is built, and a figure without a source is shown as NEEDS SOURCE rather than estimated.

Fee to a reader, excise in law. No behavioral response is assumed: data centers build the same amount with or without the fee. Revenue is held at today's buildout for every year of the endowment; no growth path is assumed.
